project.title: La La L.A.
project.subtitle: LA Through the Eyes of La La Land — a location tour of Damien Chazelle's 2016 musical
project.routeDistanceKm: approx. 130 km total driving (estimate only — verify before submission)
project.routeDuration: a full day, 8-10 hours including stops

locations.title: The Opening Freeway
locations.address: 11600 S Main St, Los Angeles, CA 90061
locations.shotFacing: Northeast (toward the property at 11600 S Main St)
locations.viewpoint: From an adjacent overpass or the shoulder, looking along the ramp curve, never from the traffic lanes themselves.
locations.shotInstruction: This is not a pedestrian stop. Photograph the interchange from a legal vantage point (an adjacent street or overpass) and keep the shot as a driving pass-by, not a stop.
locations.accessibility: No pedestrian access to the ramp itself; it is an active freeway. View only from public streets nearby, and do not stop on the freeway.
locations.summary: The film opens with drivers trapped in a freeway standstill who abandon their cars to sing and dance about chasing a dream in a city that never quite delivers on it.
locations.context: The number was filmed on the high connector ramp from the southbound Harbor (110) Freeway to the westbound Century (105) Freeway. The ramp was closed to real traffic for the shoot, and the cars were deliberately turned to face the 'wrong' direction (towards downtown) so the scene would read as a morning commute into the city.
locations.significance: It sets up the film's central tension in one shot: the gap between the sunny, cheerful surface of Los Angeles and the private frustration of the people chasing a break inside it.
locations.scene: The dancers spill out of a full line of stopped cars along the elevated ramp, using the whole width of the freeway as a stage.
locations.trivia: The ramp runs one-way away from downtown in real life; the production filmed against that flow to match the morning commute it depicts.

locations.title: Mia's Courtyard Apartments
locations.shotFacing: East, down the centerline of E. 3rd St
locations.viewpoint: From the sidewalk facing the courtyard entrance, then from the street looking east.
locations.shotInstruction: Photograph the courtyard from the sidewalk (it's a residential building — be respectful of residents) and the street dance from the same stretch of E. 3rd St.
locations.accessibility: Public street; the courtyard itself is private residential property, so stay outside the gate.
locations.summary: Mia and her three roommates get ready for a party in the courtyard of their Hollywood apartment building, then spill out into a dance number down the middle of the street.
locations.context: The building used for the exterior is the Rose Towers, a 1928 Spanish-Revival courtyard apartment complex originally named the El Cordova Apartments, in Long Beach — about 25 miles from the Hollywood setting it plays in the story. The dancers move east down E. 3rd Street for the street number.
locations.significance: It is a good example of how the film's 'Hollywood' is assembled from real places scattered across greater Los Angeles rather than filmed where the story says they are.
locations.scene: The courtyard's fountain and inward-facing units read as the classic Spanish-Revival Hollywood courtyard style, even though the building is nowhere near Hollywood.
locations.trivia: Interior shots of Mia's apartment were built as a studio set, though some reporting also points to the Langham Apartments on Normandie Ave as a possible interior source.

locations.title: The Long Walk Home
locations.short: Mia's route past two Hollywood murals
locations.address: Vine St & Argyle Ave, then 1661 Wilcox Ave, Hollywood, CA
locations.shotFacing: Multiple: east on Vine, south on Argyle, then Wilcox Ave
locations.viewpoint: Vine St just west of Argyle (Hollywood Tower Apartments), Argyle Ave at Franklin (Castle Argyle), Argyle under the 101 (Dan Collins mural), and 1661 Wilcox Ave (Tom Suriya mural).
locations.shotInstruction: Walk the route in the same order the scene does; the two murals are the payoff, so budget most of your time there rather than in between.
locations.accessibility: Public sidewalks throughout; the murals are on private building walls, viewable from the street.
locations.summary: After her car is towed outside the party, Mia walks home alone through Hollywood, passing two real murals before stopping outside a doorway where she hears Sebastian's piano.
locations.context: The walk stitches together several unrelated locations as if they were one continuous street: the north half of Vine St near the Hollywood Tower Apartments, Argyle Ave near the Castle Argyle, an untitled 1986 mural by Dan Collins on the Hollywood Bowl Self-Storage building, and the 1983 'You Are the Star' mural by Tom Suriya on Wilcox Ave — a mural roughly three miles from the first one. The doorway where she hears the piano is at 1648 Wilcox Ave, next to the second mural, though it leads only to office space in real life.
locations.significance: It shows how a single 'walk' in a film can be built from geographically distant fragments, held together only by editing and matching camera direction.
locations.scene: Watch the direction changes: east down Vine, south down Argyle under the 101 overpass, then a hard cut to Wilcox Ave, three miles away, presented as the same stretch of sidewalk.
locations.trivia: The 'You Are the Star' mural has faded significantly since it was painted in 1983; production stills and restored photographs look noticeably brighter than the mural does today.

locations.title: Lipton's (The Smoke House)
locations.short: Where Mia first hears Sebastian play
locations.shotFacing: West, entering from the lounge doorway
locations.viewpoint: Interior lounge/bar area, camera roughly where Mia stood when she walked in.
locations.shotInstruction: This is a real, operating restaurant — the respectful way to 'visit' this location is to eat there, not just photograph the entrance.
locations.summary: Drawn in by piano music, Mia steps through a doorway marked 'Lipton's' and watches a pianist play, unaware he has just been fired for straying from the boss's approved playlist.
locations.context: The fictional 'Lipton's' doorway (on Wilcox Ave) leads nowhere; the interior was actually shot inside the Smoke House, a real Burbank restaurant opened in 1946 directly across the street from Warner Bros. Studios, in its more casual lounge/bar area rather than the main dining room.
locations.significance: It's a small case study in how a film restaurant is assembled from an exterior door on one street and an interior fifteen miles away on another.
locations.scene: The scene was shot in the Smoke House's bar/lounge, dressed with white tablecloths and Christmas lights added for the film; Sebastian's piano was placed in the middle of the room rather than on the room's actual small stage.
locations.trivia: The Smoke House has been a Hollywood industry haunt since its opening night drew Bob Hope and Bing Crosby; its walls carry decades of photos of stars who have eaten there.

locations.title: Walking Between the Sound Stages
locations.short: The studio tour, and the 'I hate jazz' scene
locations.viewpoint: Between Stage 16 (right) and Stage 21 (left), heading toward The Mill.
locations.shotInstruction: Warner Bros. is a working studio, not a walk-up location — the backlot is only accessible on an official studio tour, so plan and book ahead rather than expecting street access.
locations.accessibility: Access only via a paid, scheduled Warner Bros. Studio Tour; no public walk-up access to the backlot.
locations.summary: During a tour of the studio where Mia works, Sebastian tells her to write her own roles instead of waiting to be cast in someone else's — advice that later saves her career — and she confesses she doesn't actually like jazz.
locations.context: The walk was filmed on the real Warner Bros. backlot, on Avenue D between Stage 16 and Stage 21, heading toward a facility called The Mill. Stage 16 was raised to 98 feet at the request of actress Marion Davies, making it briefly the tallest sound stage in North America; both stages have hosted decades of film and TV productions.
locations.significance: It grounds the film's fictional studio inside a real, working one, and the advice given here is a hinge point for Mia's arc in the story.
locations.scene: The two soundstages flanking the walk (16 and 21) are visibly enormous, aging industrial buildings rather than a glamorous backdrop — the ordinary machinery behind the on-screen magic.
locations.trivia: Stage 16 has hosted everything from Busby Berkeley musical numbers to a built-in-studio set of an entire park for 'The Music Man'; Stage 21 currently houses a network sitcom.

locations.title: The Lighthouse Jazz Club
locations.viewpoint: Small stage area inside the club, near the front tables.
locations.shotInstruction: Check the calendar before visiting if hearing live jazz specifically matters to you, since the booking has diversified beyond jazz.
locations.accessibility: Public venue, cover charge likely on live music nights.
locations.summary: Sebastian brings Mia to hear a live band and makes his case for improvisation and jazz; the club reappears later with Sebastian himself on piano while Mia dances.
locations.context: This is the Lighthouse Cafe, a real and historically significant jazz club that opened in 1949 and helped pioneer West Coast modern jazz through its house band, the Lighthouse All-Stars. The red-and-white striped lighthouse logo seen in the film isn't the venue's actual branding, which uses a different lighthouse mark.
locations.significance: Using a genuinely historic jazz room (rather than a set) lets the film's argument about jazz's value lean on a real institution instead of an invented one.
locations.scene: Inside, it is a small, dimly lit, brick-walled room built around the bandstand — intimate rather than glamorous.
locations.trivia: The Lighthouse still books live music most nights, but not exclusively jazz anymore — expect rock, reggae, or country depending on the night.

locations.title: The Pier
locations.viewpoint: Along the pier deck, facing the water at sunset.
locations.shotInstruction: Go at sunset to match the film's lighting mood, but expect the plain real pier rather than the lamp-lit version — that part is scene dressing, not reality.
locations.summary: Leaving Mia at the jazz club, Sebastian walks out onto a pier and sings 'City of Stars,' briefly dancing with a stranger's wife along the way.
locations.context: This is the Hermosa Beach Pier, right next to the Lighthouse Cafe. The decision to shoot here was a late change — the production originally planned to have Sebastian sing while walking past shops on Pier Ave, but switched to the pier after scouting the view. The iconic blue lamp posts seen in the shot are props; the real pier doesn't have them (though the city has since discussed adding them permanently after the film's popularity).
locations.significance: It's the clearest example in the film of a small, ordinary real place (a plain municipal pier) being transformed by lighting, props, and staging into an iconic image.
locations.scene: Compare the plain, unadorned real pier to the warmly lit, lamp-post-lined version in the film — the geometry matches, almost nothing else does.
locations.trivia: Hermosa held a 'La La Land Day' in 2017, briefly reinstalling the prop lamp posts and inviting cast members back to the pier.

locations.title: Angels Flight
locations.address: 351 S Hill St, Los Angeles, CA 90013
locations.shotFacing: Facing the ascending car, from the lower station
locations.viewpoint: Lower station looking up the track, or from the upper station looking down.
locations.shotInstruction: Ride the funicular or photograph from the station platforms. It's a short ride, but wait for the next car if you want an empty shot.
locations.accessibility: Public funicular, small fare; operating hours may vary.
films: Angels Flight has appeared in many films
locations.summary: Mia and Sebastian ride the historic Angels Flight funicular, sharing a kiss against the backdrop of downtown LA.
locations.context: Angels Flight is a historic funicular railway in the Bunker Hill district of downtown Los Angeles. It opened in 1901 and has been featured in numerous films. In La La Land, the ride is a romantic moment during the 'City of Stars' montage.
locations.significance: It's a key romantic beat, and the funicular is a symbol of the city's history and the characters' upward trajectory.
locations.scene: They board at the lower station, ride up, and kiss at the top.
locations.trivia: Angels Flight was closed for several years after a fatal accident in 2001 and reopened in 2017, shortly after the film's release.

locations.title: The Rialto Theatre
locations.address: 1401 S Oak Knoll Ave, Pasadena, CA 91106
locations.viewpoint: Fair Oaks Ave, looking at the theatre's front and marquee.
locations.shotInstruction: The theatre is currently closed to the public, so this is an exterior-only stop; check current status before planning any interior visit.
locations.accessibility: Private resort hotel; public areas accessible (lobby, grounds) but may require being a guest for full access. Check with front desk.
locations.summary: Sebastian waits inside a movie theatre during a screening of 'Rebel Without a Cause,' hoping Mia will show up after leaving a date with her boyfriend. She arrives late, they sit together, and the print breaks during the film's Griffith Observatory scene — prompting them to go there in person.
locations.context: This is the Rialto Theatre in South Pasadena (not the similarly named, now-converted Rialto in downtown L.A.'s Broadway theatre district). Opened in 1925 as a vaudeville and movie house, it closed in 2010 and has since changed hands, with community groups lobbying for its restoration. It has also appeared in 'The Player' (1992) and 'Scream 2' (1997).
locations.significance: The theatre is the hinge that sends the couple to the Observatory next, and its real, fading grandeur mirrors the film's nostalgia for classic Hollywood.
locations.scene: The vintage marquee is unchanged from its film appearance, though the theatre itself has been closed to the public since 2010.
locations.trivia: South Pasadena's residential streets (pine trees, Craftsman cottages) are a favorite stand-in for the Midwest or East Coast in other films, including 'Back to the Future' and 'Halloween.'

locations.title: The Observatory
locations.address: 2800 E Observatory Rd, Los Angeles, CA 90027
locations.shotFacing: South, approaching on the pedestrian path
locations.viewpoint: Grounds, rotunda interior, and the planetarium theatre.
locations.shotInstruction: Free admission, but the planetarium show itself (where the film's dance was staged) requires a ticket; check showtimes ahead.
locations.accessibility: Free public grounds; planetarium shows are ticketed and can sell out on busy days.
locations.summary: Following the broken film print, Mia and Sebastian visit the real Griffith Observatory, wander the planetarium, and dance a waltz that lifts them into a projected starfield.
locations.context: Griffith Observatory (built 1935, always free admission) is one of Hollywood's most recognizable filming locations, having also appeared in 'Rebel Without a Cause' (with a James Dean bust outside commemorating it), 'The Terminator,' 'Transformers,' and many others. For the floating waltz sequence, the production built a full replica of the planetarium's older Art Deco interior on a soundstage, both to recreate a since-remodeled look and to allow the wire work needed for the dancers to appear to float.
locations.significance: It's the most immediately recognizable single location in the film, and a rare case where the movie both filmed on the real site and rebuilt part of it on a stage for a single sequence.
locations.scene: The exterior grounds, rotunda, and Foucault pendulum are the real building; the floating planetarium dance itself is a studio set built to match an earlier version of the room.
locations.trivia: Over 20,000 school students visit the Observatory yearly on weekday field trips — visit on a Monday or Tuesday for a quieter experience.

locations.title: The Hilltop View
locations.address: Mount Hollywood Dr (near Cathy's Corner), Griffith Park, Los Angeles, CA
locations.shotFacing: North, into the San Fernando Valley
locations.viewpoint: The hairpin turn at Cathy's Corner, on the closed section of Mount Hollywood Dr.
locations.shotInstruction: This requires a real hike (about 2.5 miles uphill from Observatory parking) on a road closed to cars; go in daylight, with water, and do not attempt it at or after sunset given the isolation of the trail.
locations.bestTime: Daytime only — do not attempt at dusk
locations.accessibility: Foot and bicycle access only; the road is closed to vehicles. Isolated area — go in a group, bring water, and turn back well before dark.
locations.summary: After leaving a party, Mia and Sebastian find a hilltop view and half-mock, half-fall into a competitive dance number shot in a single unbroken take — the image that became the film's poster.
locations.context: The spot is known as Cathy's Corner, on a hairpin turn of Mount Hollywood Drive in Griffith Park — a section of road closed to cars and reachable only on foot, roughly a 2.5-mile uphill hike from parking near the Observatory. The bench and blue lamp post seen in the film are props, since removed; the view itself faces north into the San Fernando Valley, not the skyline or ocean the song's lyrics describe.
locations.significance: It's a good example of a single iconic 'view' shot being built from a genuinely difficult-to-reach real spot, dressed with props, and edited to imply a different, more scenic sightline than the one actually available.
locations.scene: The dance was filmed as one continuous take, with no cuts, timed to catch the actual sunset light — the production reportedly got a usable take only on the third day of trying.
locations.trivia: The road this scene appears to be on doesn't match Dorilee Lane (the party's supposed street); it is a different stretch of Mount Hollywood Drive entirely.

locations.title: The Restaurant Escape
locations.short: Mia bolts from a bad date
locations.address: Beverly Blvd & N San Vicente Blvd, Los Angeles, CA 90048
locations.shotFacing: West then north, Beverly Blvd to Harper Ave
locations.viewpoint: Interior bar area, then the sidewalk on Beverly Blvd and the roadway on Harper Ave.
locations.shotInstruction: This is a real, operating restaurant — visiting for a meal is the respectful way to see the interior; the running shot is on public sidewalks/street outside.
locations.accessibility: Public restaurant; the street scenes are on public sidewalks and roadway.
locations.summary: Bored on a date with her current boyfriend and his brother, Mia hears Sebastian's piano theme in the background, makes up her mind, and runs out of the restaurant toward the Rialto.
locations.context: The restaurant is Jar, a real 'modern American chophouse' at the corner of Beverly Blvd and Harper Ave in Beverly Grove. Mia exits and walks west along Beverly, then turns and runs north up the middle of Harper Ave — the production added the film's recurring blue lamp posts and string lights to the block for the shot.
locations.significance: It's a small, real-world beat that sets the theatre scene in motion, and it's one of the more upscale, identifiable real restaurants used in the film.
locations.scene: The interior's large hanging ceiling lamps are a distinctive, easily recognizable feature of the real restaurant, visible behind Mia at the bar as she exits.
locations.trivia: Jar has also appeared in 'Ray Donovan,' 'Modern Family,' and 'I Love You, Man.'

locations.title: The Bridge at Sunset
locations.address: W Colorado Blvd & Terrace Dr, Pasadena, CA 91105
locations.shotFacing: East-northeast, down the travel lanes toward the concrete bridge arches
locations.viewpoint: The south-side walkway of the bridge, near the S. Grand Ave cul-de-sac access point.
locations.shotInstruction: Approach on foot from the north end of S. Grand Ave; the bridge carries real traffic, so stay on the walkway and be cautious near the roadway edge.
locations.accessibility: Public walkway alongside active vehicle traffic; the surrounding streets are a confusing tangle of freeway on/off-ramps, so plan the walking approach rather than trying to park directly on the bridge.
locations.summary: A brief shot of Mia and Sebastian strolling at dusk along a bridge lit with globe lights, mountains visible behind them, part of the film's summer-romance montage.
locations.context: This is the Colorado Street Bridge in Pasadena, built in 1912 and, at the time, the tallest concrete bridge in the world. It is on the National Register of Historic Places, known for its distinctive 50-degree curve (a practical solution for spanning the Arroyo Seco gorge) and its Beaux Arts arches.
locations.significance: It's a genuinely historic Pasadena landmark used for a fleeting, purely romantic montage beat rather than a scene tied to any specific plot point.
locations.scene: The couple walks west along the bridge's south sidewalk; the globe lighting along the walkway is real, part of the bridge's own historic lighting.
locations.trivia: The bridge has an unfortunate, well-documented history of suicides, and is on record as one of the most-used bridges in the U.S. for that purpose — worth knowing if you plan to walk it, and a reason to treat a visit respectfully.

locations.title: The Food Hall
locations.viewpoint: Sarita's Pupuseria, stall E-5, near the market's Broadway-side entrance.
locations.shotInstruction: Come outside lunch rush to avoid long lines; the market opens at 10 AM.
locations.accessibility: Public market, open daily; can be crowded at lunchtime.
locations.summary: Another brief montage beat: Mia and Sebastian share a meal on stools inside a large, neon-lit food hall.
locations.context: This is Grand Central Market, opened in 1917, a large hall of roughly three dozen food stalls in downtown L.A. The specific counter used in the shot is Sarita's Pupuseria (stall E-5). The market sits directly across the street from the Bradbury Building (used in 'Blade Runner') and near Angels Flight — notably, Ryan Gosling later starred in 'Blade Runner 2049.'
locations.significance: It shows the film using a genuinely lived-in, working-class downtown institution for a purely atmospheric montage moment, in contrast to the more staged or historic locations elsewhere in the story.
locations.scene: The blue neon at Sarita's Pupuseria matches the shot; the market's mix of international food stalls under one warehouse-like roof is real and largely unchanged for the scene.
locations.trivia: Grand Central Market originally served Bunker Hill's wealthy residents, who rode Angels Flight down the hill to shop there before that neighborhood's Victorian homes were demolished for today's skyscrapers.

locations.title: The Palm Trees
locations.address: 1000 Vin Scully Ave, Los Angeles, CA 90012
locations.shotFacing: East-southeast, past the security kiosk toward the stadium
locations.viewpoint: Park Drive, near its intersection area northwest of Dodger Stadium.
locations.shotInstruction: Go near sunset to match the silhouette look of the shot; parking is easiest on non-game days when Dodger Stadium traffic is light.
locations.accessibility: Public park roads; avoid Dodger Stadium game days when nearby traffic is heavy.
locations.summary: A brief, silhouette shot of a long row of tall palm trees against the sunset — the archetypal 'Los Angeles' image used in countless films.
locations.context: The palms line Elysian Park Road (also called Angels Point Road) in Elysian Park, just north of downtown next to Dodger Stadium, near the popular Angels Point lookout. The shot itself was taken from a different nearby road, Park Drive, looking east.
locations.significance: It's the film using one of the single most over-photographed 'L.A. establishing shot' images in movies, tying its own visual language to a much larger tradition of L.A. filmmaking.
locations.scene: The palms themselves are on Elysian Park Road, but the classic silhouette photo is taken from Park Drive, a short distance away — worth knowing if you're trying to recreate the exact frame.
locations.trivia: Elysian Park sits directly beside Dodger Stadium and is a popular, easy-access filming location compared to the more remote spots elsewhere in this tour.

route.title: One-Day Reel Road
route.description: A practical, geography-first route for visiting as many locations as reasonably possible in a single day, grouped by neighborhood.

screen.title: Screen Order
screen.description: The order these places appear on screen, by timestamp, from the film's opening number to its final montage. This is the tour's required chronological narrative, reinterpreted for a single-film project as the film's own internal timeline rather than a historical period sequence.
